questions.stem: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro were the largest cities of which civilisation?
options: The Mauryan Empire of the emperor Ashoka
The Vedic kingdoms of the great Ganges plain
The Gupta Empire of northern India
The Indus Valley (Harappan) civilisation
questions.explanation: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, in present-day Pakistan, flourished around 2600–1900 BCE as part of the Indus Valley civilisation, one of the world's earliest urban societies alongside Egypt and Mesopotamia. The Vedic, Mauryan and Gupta periods all came later, and the Mauryan and Gupta empires were centred on the Ganges plain.

questions.stem: Which feature of Mohenjo-daro most impresses archaeologists?
options: Enormous royal palaces and richly furnished tombs for its kings
Great stone pyramids built as burial places for its rulers
Temple walls carved with long written histories of its many battles
Streets laid out in a grid, with covered drains and brick houses
questions.explanation: Mohenjo-daro had planned streets, standard-sized baked bricks, houses with bathrooms and a citywide drainage system, as well as the Great Bath, a large waterproofed brick pool. Surprisingly, archaeologists have found no grand palaces or royal tombs, which makes it hard to know who ruled. The Indus script survives only on short seals and small objects.

questions.stem: Why do historians still know relatively little about the government and beliefs of the Indus Valley civilisation?
options: It left no objects except broken pottery
All its buildings were wooden and have rotted
Its script has never been deciphered
None of its cities have yet been excavated
questions.explanation: Thousands of short inscriptions survive on seals, but no bilingual text like the Rosetta Stone has been found and the inscriptions are too short to crack, so the language remains unknown. Archaeologists have excavated many Indus sites, finding seals, jewellery, weights, toys and tools in cities built of baked brick. Everything known about the society comes from this material evidence.

questions.stem: Why was the summer monsoon so important to farmers in ancient India?
options: Its dry winds ripened crops quickly before the floods came
Its heavy rains watered the crops and filled the rivers
Its winds carried fertile silt from the Himalaya onto fields
It brought winter snow that farmers melted for irrigation
questions.explanation: From about June to September, monsoon winds bring most of India's yearly rain, feeding crops such as rice and swelling the Indus, the Ganges and other rivers. If the monsoon failed, famine could follow, so farming life was organised around it. Fertile silt is carried by the rivers, not blown by the wind.

questions.stem: The Vedas, the oldest sacred texts of Hinduism, were composed in which language?
options: Persian
Sanskrit
Pali
Tamil
questions.explanation: The Vedas, including the Rigveda, were composed in an early form of Sanskrit and passed down by memory and recitation for many centuries before being written down. Pali is the language of many early Buddhist scriptures, and Tamil is a separate language of southern India with its own ancient literature. Sanskrit later became a language of learning across much of South and South-East Asia.

questions.stem: In the varna system, which group were the priests and teachers?
options: Kshatriyas
Vaishyas
Shudras
Brahmins
questions.explanation: The four varnas were the Brahmins (priests and teachers), Kshatriyas (rulers and warriors), Vaishyas (farmers, herders and traders) and Shudras (labourers and servants). Groups placed outside the varnas, later called 'untouchables', faced the harshest discrimination. Discrimination by caste was outlawed in India's constitution of 1950.

questions.stem: According to the Purusha hymn in the Rigveda, where did the four varnas come from?
options: Four rivers flowing down from the peaks of the Himalaya
Four eggs laid by a golden bird at the very start of time
Different parts of the body of a cosmic being, Purusha
Four sons born to Manu, the first human after the flood
questions.explanation: The hymn describes the gods sacrificing Purusha, with the Brahmins coming from his mouth, the Kshatriyas from his arms, the Vaishyas from his thighs and the Shudras from his feet. This origin story was later used to justify ranking the varnas from highest to lowest. Manu appears in a different story, as the man saved from a great flood.

questions.stem: How did jati differ from varna in ancient Indian society?
options: Jati were many local birth groups, often linked to a particular job
Jati were the four broad classes described in the sacred Vedas
Jati were groups that a person could choose to join by passing an examination
Jati were the ranks of priests within the Brahmin varna alone
questions.explanation: Varna was a broad four-part scheme, but daily life was shaped more by jati, thousands of hereditary groups often linked to an occupation such as potter or weaver, which set rules about marriage, food and social contact. People were born into their jati and normally married within it. The four broad classes are the varnas themselves.

questions.stem: In Hindu belief, what is karma?
options: The cycle of birth, death and rebirth itself
The idea that a person's actions shape their future lives
Release from the endless cycle of birth, death and rebirth
A person's duty according to their place in society
questions.explanation: Karma is the principle that good and bad actions have consequences, affecting a person's rebirth. Samsara is the cycle of rebirth, dharma is a person's duty and right conduct, and moksha is release from samsara, the ultimate goal. Many Hindus see Brahman, the ultimate reality, as present in all things, which links belief with respect for the natural world.

questions.stem: In the Hindu flood story, how was Manu saved from the great flood?
options: A fish he had protected warned him and towed his boat to safety
An eagle carried him to the top of the Himalaya before the waters rose
The Buddha told him to build a great ark for all of the animals
He climbed a giant banyan tree that grew above the floodwaters
questions.explanation: Manu saved a small fish, which grew huge and warned him of the coming flood; it then towed his boat to a mountain, and in later versions the fish is the god Vishnu in the form of Matsya. Manu went on to become the ancestor of humanity. The Buddha plays no part in this Vedic story.

questions.stem: According to Buddhist tradition, Siddhartha Gautama grew up as:
options: a merchant who travelled the trade routes to Persia
a prince who left his palace to seek an end to suffering
a Brahmin priest who composed hymns of the Rigveda
a Mauryan emperor who gave up war after a terrible battle
questions.explanation: Tradition says the young prince saw old age, sickness and death, gave up his comfortable life and, after years of searching, reached enlightenment and became the Buddha, 'the awakened one'. The emperor who gave up war after a battle was Ashoka, who lived about two centuries later and helped spread Buddhism.

questions.stem: The Buddha's Four Noble Truths teach that suffering is caused by:
options: craving and attachment
the anger of the gods
being born a Shudra
neglecting Vedic rituals
questions.explanation: The Four Noble Truths state that life involves suffering, that suffering comes from craving and attachment, that it can end, and that the way to end it is the Noble Eightfold Path of right understanding, right speech, right action and so on. The Buddha rejected the idea that birth into a varna decided a person's spiritual worth, and he did not teach that elaborate rituals were needed.

questions.stem: Jainism places great importance on ahimsa. What does ahimsa mean?
options: Worship of a single creator god
Bathing in the sacred river Ganges
Passing through the four stages of a person's life
Non-violence towards all living things
questions.explanation: Jains try to avoid harming any living being, so many are strict vegetarians and some monks sweep the path in front of them to avoid treading on insects. Jainism, taught by Mahavira around the same time as the Buddha, does not teach a creator god. Ahimsa also became important in Buddhism and Hinduism, and much later inspired Mahatma Gandhi.

questions.stem: In ancient India, what did the sacred thread ceremony (upanayana) mark?
options: A young couple's marriage, as they walked around a sacred fire
The cremation of a relative on the bank of a river
A new king being crowned and anointed by the priests
A boy of the upper varnas beginning his religious education
questions.explanation: In upanayana a boy from the Brahmin, Kshatriya or Vaishya varna received a sacred thread worn over the shoulder and began studying the Vedas with a teacher, a ceremony seen as a second birth. Walking around a sacred fire is part of the Hindu marriage ceremony, and the usual funeral rite was cremation, with the ashes often placed in a river.

questions.stem: Alexander the Great invaded north-western India in 326 BCE. Why did his campaign there come to an end?
options: Monsoon floods drowned most of his army on the Indus
His exhausted soldiers refused to march any further east
He was killed in battle by the Indian king Porus
Chandragupta Maurya drove him out of the city of Pataliputra
questions.explanation: After defeating Porus at the Hydaspes River, Alexander wanted to push on, but at the Beas (Hyphasis) River his army, worn out after years of fighting, refused to go further, and he turned back; he died in Babylon in 323 BCE. Two centuries earlier the Persian Empire under Darius I had already ruled the Indus region. Soon after Alexander left, Chandragupta Maurya took over the north-west.

questions.stem: Who founded the Mauryan Empire around 321 BCE?
options: Siddhartha Gautama
Chandragupta Maurya
Ashoka
Chandragupta I
questions.explanation: Chandragupta Maurya overthrew the Nanda kingdom of Magadha and built an empire across northern India, with its capital at Pataliputra. Ashoka was his grandson. Chandragupta I, with a similar name, founded the Gupta Empire more than 600 years later, in the 300s CE.

questions.stem: The Arthashastra, traditionally said to be by Kautilya (Chanakya), adviser to Chandragupta Maurya, is a guide to:
options: the teachings of the Buddha on how to end suffering
medicine, surgery and the use of healing herbs
running a state, including taxes, laws, war and spies
the rules of the varnas for marriage and for daily life
questions.explanation: The Arthashastra sets out in practical detail how a king should collect taxes, run a government, keep law and order, use spies and wage war, showing how organised Mauryan rule was meant to be. Rules for the varnas and daily life are found in law books such as the Laws of Manu. Scholars think the text was added to over several centuries.

questions.stem: What led the emperor Ashoka to turn to Buddhism and rule by 'dhamma'?
options: His horror at the killing and suffering of the Kalinga war
His defeat in battle by the army of Alexander the Great
Meeting the Buddha himself, who was still teaching during his reign
A famine that killed most of his family and his court
questions.explanation: In one of his own edicts Ashoka expresses deep regret for the war in Kalinga, in which he says a great many people were killed or deported. Afterwards he promoted dhamma: non-violence, tolerance and care for people and animals. Alexander died before Ashoka was born, and the Buddha had lived about two centuries earlier.

questions.stem: How did Ashoka spread his messages about dhamma across his empire?
options: With laws painted on the walls of the Great Bath
With songs taught to soldiers marching to each city
With edicts carved on rocks and tall stone pillars
With books printed on paper and sent to every town
questions.explanation: Ashoka's edicts were carved in local languages and scripts, such as Brahmi and, in the north-west, Greek and Aramaic, so people across the empire could have them read aloud. The Lion Capital from one of his pillars, at Sarnath, is now India's national emblem. Paper and printing came to India many centuries later.

questions.stem: According to tradition, Ashoka's son Mahinda carried Buddhism to which land?
options: Sri Lanka
Japan
Tibet
Arabia
questions.explanation: Sri Lankan chronicles record that Mahinda, a Buddhist monk, brought the teaching to Sri Lanka, where Theravada Buddhism remains the main religion. From India, Buddhism later spread along trade routes to Central Asia, China, Korea and Japan. It did not reach Japan until the 500s CE or Tibet until the 600s CE.

questions.stem: Indian mathematicians, including those of the Gupta period, helped develop a decimal place-value system. Which modern system grew from it?
options: The numerals 0 to 9 used around the world today
Roman numerals such as X, L, C and M
The metric system of metres and kilograms
Measuring time in hours that are made up of sixty minutes
questions.explanation: Mathematicians such as Aryabhata used place value, and zero came to be used as a number in India; these numerals passed to the Arab world and then to Europe, which is why they are called Hindu–Arabic numerals. Roman numerals came from Rome, the metric system from France in the 1790s, and the 60-minute hour from ancient Mesopotamia.

questions.stem: Large hoards of Roman gold and silver coins have been found in southern India. What do they show?
options: Indian kings sent tribute to the Roman emperor every year
Roman coins were the official money of the Mauryan Empire
Roman merchants paid in coin for Indian goods such as pepper
Rome conquered southern India and ruled it for a long time
questions.explanation: Trade across the Indian Ocean, using the monsoon winds, carried pepper, spices, gems and cotton cloth to Rome, and Roman writers complained about how much gold flowed east to pay for them. Rome never ruled any part of India, and this trade boomed only after the Mauryan Empire had ended. India also traded overland with China.

questions.stem: Modern India uses Ashoka's Lion Capital as its national emblem and his wheel on its flag. Why might a modern nation choose these symbols?
options: Ashoka drove the British out of India in the ancient past
Ashoka wrote India's first constitution on his stone pillars
Ashoka is remembered as a unifier who ruled with tolerance and peace
Ashoka founded Hinduism, the religion of most Indians today
questions.explanation: Ashoka ruled most of the subcontinent and is remembered for edicts calling for tolerance between religions and kindness to all, values India's leaders wanted to highlight after independence in 1947. Hinduism has no single founder, and Ashoka promoted Buddhism. His edicts were moral messages, not a constitution.
